content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a methodology for training prediction models that, at test time, have access to some of the full set of features available at training time. More precisely, it is assumed that the model has access to a set of “machine features” both during training and testing, and that it can query B of the available “human features” during deployment. Two related methods are proposed for training and their performance is presented in experiments on two datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper tackles an interesting problem. However, I see the following issues.

With respect to the methods, I don’t fully understand how the proposed method differs from forward selection methods (stepwise regression) other than for the fact that it is assumed that a subset of the features is always available and the problem is only to find which of the remaining features should be considered in the prediction. This seems to be the procedure that the authors use in the optimization and, if this is the case, then I am not sure what the contribution of this method to the existing literature is. The authors also make the assumption that human features are independent conditionally on machine features in (3). While this assumption is unlikely to hold in practice, there is no discussion of that.  

With respect to the experiments, the authors seem to handpick the features that will be missing at test time. This choice may easily explain the observed results (higher performance of the proposed methods), as giving the model access to a few good predictors through a couple of queries would boost model performance. Instead, the authors could have randomly chosen (and repeated this many times) the two sets of features (human and machine) and reported those results. That would have been a more fair comparison in my opinion. 
I also think that the experiments are missing an important comparison: The one with some human features being imputed from the machine features at test time, without querying the human at all. There are a wide array of methods that can do this, and that are not based on the independence assumption made by the authors (which is limiting). My understanding is that the proposed method will be most useful when the machine features are uncorrelated with the human features (otherwise we could easily impute those feature and the predictors ), but there is not discussion of this. This seems to be a very important consideration underlying the paper. The authors could provide more details on when their method would be most useful and should be used. The paper lacks these details at the moment.
Relatedly, some examples of applications are missing. The authors could provide real-world contexts where they believe their method would be useful. Experiments with human subjects would also be useful. 

Details:
* Although I understand the meaning, I find the notation in (3) confusing: On the LHS f^{marg} is also over q and on the RHS p is conditioned on q. In addition, x_h only appears on the LHS and not on the RHS. 
* On the RHS of (5), x_h shows up again. 
* “MTurk responses” were mentioned in 5.1. Did humans participate in these experiments? If so, more details about the experiment should be provided. 
* There are some typos in the paper. Three examples: \tilde{x}^m_d in (4) should be \tilde{x}^m, I believe; “models associations between…”; “it this set”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper was fairly clear. Experimental section includes some details (not all that would be needed for reproducibility), and no code was provided. Quality and novelty were discussed above.
content.summary_of_the_review: I have detailed my concerns regarding some of the limitations of the paper, that I hope the authors can address.

content.title: Thank you for your review
content.comment:
Thank you for your thorough and helpful review!  

The main difference between this and the feature selection methods you mention is that the selected features are individual to each instance rather than doing feature selection for the entire dataset at once.  We'll clarify that point in the writing.

You're right that the independence between the human features is an assumption that may often not hold in practice.  It's intended as an approximation of the true distribution, but we will emphasize that in the writing.

The machine-only baseline marginalizes out the missing human features, so is equivalent to doing feature imputation with the assumption that the human features are independent.  We'll consider exploring feature imputation methods that don't make this assumption.

Thank you for your suggestions on further experiments.  We'll consider these, and also emphasize in the writing when one can expect this approach to work.  We can generally expect it to be useful when Xm gives us some information about Xh but doesn't fully predict Xh.  If there's no correlation between Xm and Xh, p(Xh|Xm) won't be that informative, and if they're fully correlated, then Xh doesn't provide any additional information to improve the prediction.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tackles the problem of which features should be sampled at test time to best improve predictive performances at an individual level. The proposed method consists of an entropy-based strategy. This approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performances under a constrained number of queries.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is really clear and well structured with interesting experimentation. 

However, the paper presents major limitations:
- The absence of multi-arm bandit references. The entropy-based approach is a simple multi-arm bandit approach that has been studied and improved. More importantly, the studied problem has a large literature that is not mentioned, the problem is known as 'active feature value acquisition', 'active sensing', 'active feature elicitation', 'dynamic feature selection'... 
- The assumption that one sample all features at once is limiting. An iterative sampling may lead to a different $q$ particularly in the presence of colinearities, i.e. why is $P(x^h_d | x) = P(x^h_d | x^m)$? 
- The absence of interaction and the simplicity of the model questions the complexity of the methodology, which seems to have a closed-form solution, something like abs(uncertainty variable * weight variable)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and clear. However, the studied problem has been proposed and studied previously which weakens the main claims of this paper.

A few questions:
- How are the sets created in the experiments? The authors should perform experiments to evaluate the sensitivity to this split choice.
- What happens when no machine features are available? 
- (4) $x^m$ should not depend on $d$
content.summary_of_the_review: A well-written paper that studies an important problem but ignores a large literature on this problem with multiple solutions and datasets.

content.title: Thank you for your review
content.comment:
Thank you for your thorough and helpful review!  

We will thoroughly address the citations you mentioned in future versions of this work.  Briefly, some of these approaches solve a different problem of either finding the feature values to fill in at train time (e.g. [5]), or finding the set of instances to fully fill in the values for at test time (e.g. [4]).  Some solve a similar problem using different methodology that learns which features to query for test instances based on train instances (e.g. [1], [2], [3]).  None are specifically targeted to the case we study of users filling in their own features to improve predictions made about them, but it's a fair question which of these approaches is most appropriate in that setting.

The assumption that the p(Xh) depends only on Xm is an approximation that appears to work reasonably in practice.  We'll make that clearer in the writing.

The closed form you mentioned isn't exactly equivalent because the predicted probability before querying Xh also matters, but we agree that this would be a useful baseline/ablation to test.

Citations:
[1] Kanani, P., & Melville, P. (2008). Prediction-time active feature-value acquisition for cost-effective customer targeting. Advances in neural information processing systems (NIPS).
[2] Sheng, V. S., & Ling, C. X. (2006, June). Feature value acquisition in testing: a sequential batch test algorithm. In Proceedings of the 23rd international conference on Machine learning (pp. 809-816).
[3] Das, S., Iyer, R., & Natarajan, S. (2021). A clustering based selection framework for cost aware and test-time feature elicitation. In 8th ACM IKDD CODS and 26th COMAD (pp. 20-28).
[4] Sankaranarayanan, K., & Dhurandhar, A. (2013, October). Intelligently querying incomplete instances for improving classification performance. In Proceedings of the 22nd ACM international conference on Information & Knowledge Management (pp. 2169-2178).
[5] Saar-Tsechansky, M., Melville, P., & Provost, F. (2009). Active feature-value acquisition. Management Science, 55(4), 664-684.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Summary: The paper proposes a novel approach for integrating experts in into the prediction process of supervised learning algorithms. The setting targets situations where, at test time, important features might be costly and not available by default. As such, a query budget limits the number of features one can ask for. The setting makes another specialization: Situations are targeted for which the user of the algorithm is not the expert of the domain. The authors solve the problem by defining a constrained optimization problem to find the minimal set of features to query to minimize model uncertainty. At training time all features are assumed to be available. This also enables to learn an expectation of the feature values, which is used for the optimization at test time. The approach is evaluated for for two kaggel datasets against an oracle basline which gets all features, a minimal baseline which only gets so-called machine features and a standard feature selection algorithm which proposed a fixed set of features. The results show that the proposed approach is competitive or superior to standard feature selection and always better than the minimum number of features.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* Well-defined approach and thorough description of the details of the optimization process
* Thorough evaluation results for the two datasets

Weaknesses:
* The method assumes full access of features at training time (the authors also shortly discuss this wrt future directions in the paper)- there might be approaches which already try to limit this during during training set collection.  
* The evaluation is, while thorough for the present datasets, limited to two datasets. It would be helpful to motivate why these have been chosen. As the authors assume full knowledge of all features at training time, it would even more help the paper to show the added value of the line of approaches on more datasets.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: High clarity, as the paper is well-written, well-motivated and clearly defines the components of the approach.
Quality: The taken approach for solving the problem is adequate and well introduced. The results of the evaluation are also sufficient, although the approach is rather on par with feature selection for birds dataset.
Novelty: The authors make a good case for novelty with respect to related works on user-centered machine learning settings. 
Reproducibility: The method and parameters are clear, but code is missing. But it should be possible to reimplementm as base learners were used from scikit-learn
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach is well-motivated and thoroughly described. The paper is very clear and successfully shows where the method is situated in the State-of-the-Art. I still find that the evaluation, while deep for two datasets, could be applied to more datasets. It would also strenghen the quality of the paper, as this is the first step towards such an approach with relatively limiting assumptions (all features available at training time). Finally, I am wondering about possible extensions of the approach wrt real-world scenarios, such as limited availability of features.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
